explanation: Mangum cites Tanner only as a 'see also' noting it presumed without deciding that the mandate rule reaches agencies; supporting, non-controlling authority. Tanner itself states it is unpublished and not binding.

Beuns says the facts 'fit squarely within our precedent, which holds' the $500-per-device rule, citing only unpublished Gilmore, and affirms on it; a different defendant and case. Unpublished Sixth Circuit opinions are not binding.
Slusser mentions Page only as a case the petitioner cited and expressly distinguishes it (plea voluntariness challenge); it is not followed, let alone treated as controlling.
Lumaj cites Hasanaj in a footnote only to show counsel had notice the argument was rejected; the court names published Denko as the controlling precedent, not Hasanaj.

Barbourville cites Livingston as 388 F.3d 168, the published version of that opinion (own knowledge: the F. App'x decision was later published), and merely quotes it describing the regulation's preventive focus, in the text given.

Ochoa-Perez, an Anders dismissal, is never cited; the citation at 614 F. App'x 789 is to Bach v. Texas State University, a different decision sharing the page. Though the court calls its unpublished decisions 'our precedent', the named decision was not relied on.
Brand Services cites Curry with a parenthetical as an example of discretion to deny untimely motions to compel, then rules the other way on published authority; illustrative, not controlling.
